title: Introduction (EEFP)
shortDescription: Start building confident, everyday English for school, home, and community life. In this short kickoff, you’ll learn simple phrases for parent–teacher talks, WhatsApp/notice replies, and daily routines—plus quick pronunciation tips and a mini practice task to use with your child today.
summary: This kickoff lesson orients parents to the course goals and shows how to use simple, practical English in daily family and school situations. Learners review key phrases for greetings, scheduling, parent–teacher messages, and WhatsApp/notice replies; practice clear pronunciation of names, dates, and numbers; and learn polite question forms (“Could you…?”, “Would you mind…?”). A short role-play and a mini writing task (a message to a teacher) build confidence. By the end, parents can introduce themselves, confirm times, ask for help or clarification, and support their child’s routines using clear, polite English. A quick self-check list and take-home practice card help them apply the language immediately.
topics: Why using English at home benefits both parents and children.
How to overcome fear of speaking imperfect English.
The power of small, consistent daily practice.
How this course will help you step-by-step.
The importance of starting, not being perfect.

faq.answer: No, this course is made for absolute beginners.

faq.answer: Absolutely. Making mistakes is part of learning.

title: Greeting & Routine Talk (EEFP)
shortDescription: Learn to use English for morning routines and daily greetings with your child.
summary: This lesson helps parents use clear, polite English for everyday interactions at school and home. You’ll practice friendly greetings, small talk, and quick check-ins (hello, introducing yourself, confirming your child’s name/class). We cover routine topics—drop-off/pick-up times, homework reminders, absence/late notes, and arranging a short meeting—with simple model sentences and polite question forms (“Could we…?”, “Would it be okay if…?”). A pronunciation mini focuses on names, dates, and times. You’ll role-play a parent–teacher chat, send a short WhatsApp-style message, and complete a mini checklist to personalize phrases for your child’s routine. By the end, you can start and end conversations naturally, ask for clarification, and confirm next steps with confidence.
topics: Simple morning greetings and phrases.
English commands used during school preparation.
How to say common instructions naturally.

Building habit through consistent morning use.

faq.answer: Yes, the phrases are simple and suitable for all ages.

faq.title: What if my child replies in Bangla?
faq.answer: That’s okay. Keep speaking English, they’ll pick it up gradually.

title: Meals & Kitchen Talk (EEFP)
shortDescription: Use meal times as a natural opportunity to speak English at home.
summary:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to turn everyday mealtimes into fun and natural opportunities to speak English at home. We’ll cover useful phrases for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, how to encourage healthy eating in English, and simple ways to ask about food preferences.


You’ll discover how to build daily routines using repeated phrases like “Time to eat!” or “Do you want more?” and how to include English in cooking and meal prep. Even if extended family is present, you can still use 1–2 simple English sentences each day to make steady progress.


By the end, you’ll know how to make the kitchen a language-rich space where your child can learn and practice English every day.
topics: Useful phrases for breakfast, lunch, and dinner.
Encouraging your child to eat healthy using English.
Asking meal preferences in English.
Building routine through repeated phrases.
Making English part of everyday kitchen conversations.
How to practice during meal prep and dining.

faq.title: Can I use English if we eat with extended family?
faq.answer: Yes, you can start with simple phrases regardless of who is present.

faq.title: Do I need to translate everything?
faq.answer: No, just try using 1–2 new English sentences each day.

title: Emotions & Encouragement (EEFP)
shortDescription: Learn to express love, pride, and care for your child using comforting English phrases.
summary:
This lesson focuses on using English to express love, care, and emotional support for your child. You'll learn comforting phrases that show encouragement, pride, and belief, as well as gentle ways to respond to your child’s feelings like sadness, anger, or stress.

By modeling calm, respectful communication, you help your child build emotional intelligence and feel safe. Even if they don’t fully understand at first, repeated kind words in English will create strong emotional and language connections over time.
topics: Phrases to comfort and support your child emotionally.
How to show pride and belief in your child.
Managing sadness, anger, or stress with kind words.
Teaching emotional intelligence through language.
Role modeling calm, respectful communication.
Creating a safe space through words.

shortDescription: Turn family moments into chances to talk and bond in English.
summary:
In this lesson, you’ll learn how to use everyday family moments to build English skills and stronger connections. Discover simple phrases to talk about your child’s day, discuss school, and enjoy fun conversations together.


We’ll show you how to create meaningful exchanges in easy English, improve listening and speaking habits, and make language learning a shared family experience, one small step at a time.

Asking your child about their day in English.

Strengthening family bonds through language.

section.title: Test Text
section.text:
Dhaka Cityscape

Except Old Dhaka, which is an old bazaar-style neighbourhood, the layout of the city follows a grid pattern with organic development influenced by traditional South Asian as well as Middle Eastern and Western patterns. Growth of the city is largely unplanned and is focused on the northern regions and around the city centre, where many of the more affluent neighbourhoods may be found. Most of the construction in the city consists of concrete high-rise buildings. Middle-class and upper-class housing, along with commercial and industrial areas, occupy most of the city. However, nearly one third of Dhaka's population lives in slums, as of 2016.


Dhaka does not have a well-defined central business district. Old Dhaka is the historic commercial centre, but most development has moved to the north. In 1985, the area around Motijheel was considered the "modern" CBD, while by 2005 Gulshan was considered the "newest" part of the CBD. Many Bangladeshi government institutions can be found in Motijheel, Segunbagicha, Tejgaon, Karwan Bazar, and Sher-e-Bangla Nagar.


Much activity is centred around a few large roads, where road laws are rarely obeyed and street vendors and beggars are frequently encountered.


For much of recent history, Dhaka was characterized by roadside markets and small shops that sold a wide variety of goods. Recent years have seen the widespread construction of shopping malls. Two of the largest shopping malls in the city and the wider South Asian region are the Jamuna Future Park and Bashundhara City.

title: Facts & Techniques
shortDescription: This lesson introduces parents to two powerful communication strategies that can transform how they interact with their children and approach English learning. Through insightful video content, parents will discover why purposeful communication matters and how to start building their English vocabulary step by step — one word at a time.
summary:
Golden Circle Rule for Parent Communication

  • Understand the “Why → How → What” framework for effective communication with children.
  • Learn how purpose-driven language builds trust, motivation, and better emotional connection.
  • Practical examples of applying the Golden Circle when giving instructions or encouragement.


One Word, One Day – Start Your Journey

  • Encourages parents to begin their English learning journey in small, consistent steps.
  • Introduces the concept of learning just one word a day to build confidence and routine.
  • Shows how small habits can lead to long-term language improvement — especially for busy parents.

faq.title: Is this method easy to follow?
faq.answer: Yes, it uses simple English and real-life examples parents can apply at home.

faq.title: Why should I learn this framework?
faq.answer: It helps you communicate with purpose and build stronger family bonds.

faq.title: Do I need to memorize the phrases?
faq.answer: No, practice them regularly and they’ll become part of your natural speech.
